questions.problem:
$$

Consider the curve $x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=2.$ Given that $x=x(t),\text{ }y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ on the curve at the point $(4,\frac{\pi }{3}),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point. Do not round the answer.

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6,$ $x=4,$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{3},$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 6\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 6\cdot \frac{1}{2}-4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 3-2\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the parabola ${x}^{2}-8y=0.$ Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{8}$ on the curve at the point $(4,2),$ find the value of  $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-8y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}-8y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(8y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{8},$ $x=4,$ and $y=2,$ and solve $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot (4))-(\frac{1}{8})\cdot 8 & =0 \\ 8\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-1 & =0 \\ 8\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

Consider the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y=0.$ Given that $x=x(t),\text{ }y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=5$ on the curve at the point $(1,0),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{x}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=5,$ $x=1,$ and $y=0,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{x}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 5\cdot \frac{1}{1}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 5+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve ${e}^{x}+\operatorname{cos}⁡y=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3$ on the curve at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x}+\operatorname{cos}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3,$ $x=0,$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ and solve $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot {e}^{0}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) & =0 \\ 3+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ (-1)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-20x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}-20x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{10},$ $x=5,$ and $y=10,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 20 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot 10)-(\frac{3}{10})\cdot 20 & =0 \\ 20\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-6 & =0 \\ 20\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve ${x}^{3}-4{y}^{2}-2y=2.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $y=1,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{y}^{2}-2y & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{2}-2y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{y}^{2}+2y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4{y}^{2}+2y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (3{x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (8y+2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2$ and $y=1.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (3{x}^{2})-2\cdot 10 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $y=1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4\cdot {1}^{2}-2\cdot 1 & =2 \\ {x}^{3}-6 & =2 \\ {x}^{3} & =8 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3\cdot {2}^{2}-20 & =0 \\ 12\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =20 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve $-{y}^{3}+2(x-2)^{2}=10.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}$ on the curve at the point where $x=3,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{3}+2(x-2)^{2} & =10 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{y}^{3}+2(x-2)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2(x-2)^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(-{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2(x-2)^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-3{y}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4(x-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}$ and $x=3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-3{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4(3-2) & =0 \\ (-3{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=3$ into the equation of the curve. 

At the point where $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{3}+2(3-2)^{2} & =10 \\ -{y}^{3}+2 & =10 \\ {y}^{3} & =-8 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3(-2)^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ -12\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve ${e}^{x}-{e}^{y}=y.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3$ on the curve at the point where $y=0,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}-{e}^{y} & =y \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x}-{e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{x}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{y} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{y}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3$ and $y=0.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot {e}^{x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{0}+1) \\ -3{e}^{x} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=0$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}-{e}^{y} & =y \\ {e}^{x}-{e}^{0} & =0 \\ {e}^{x}-1 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{0} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\ -3 & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve $x+\operatorname{ln}⁡y=4.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-1$ on the curve at the point where $x=4,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x+\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-1$ and $x=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=4$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =4 \\ 4+\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2y & =-x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}+2y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}+2y) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y+2) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y+2) & =-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2$ and $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y+2) & =-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2y & =-x \\ {y}^{2}+2y & =-1 \\ {y}^{2}+2y+1 & =0 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y+2) & =-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(2\cdot (-1)+2) & =-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(0) & =-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 0 & =-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{16})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2y}{25}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $y=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{16})+3\cdot (\frac{2(3)}{25}) & =0 \\ \frac{x}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{18}{25} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=3$ into the equation of the ellipse.  

At the point where $y=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{9}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{16}{25} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{256}{25} \\ x & =\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $x>0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{16}{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{18}{25} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{8}(\frac{16}{5})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{18}{25} & =0 \\ \frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{18}{25} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{18}{25}\cdot \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{9})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2y}{9}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=12$ and $x=-5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12\cdot (\frac{2(-5)}{9})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2y}{9}) & =0 \\ -\frac{120}{9}-\frac{2y}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-5$ into the equation of the hyperbola.

At the point where $x=-5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(-5)^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{25}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ 25-{y}^{2} & =9 \\ {y}^{2} & =16 \\ y & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the second quadrant.

Finally, substituting $y=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{120}{9}-\frac{2(4)}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ -\frac{120}{9}-\frac{8}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ -\frac{8}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{120}{9} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{120}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4y & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}-4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $y=3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)-(3)\cdot 4 & =0 \\ 2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-12 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=3$ into the equation of  the parabola.  

At the point where $y=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4y & =4 \\ {x}^{2}-4\cdot (3) & =4 \\ {x}^{2}-12 & =4 \\ {x}^{2} & =16 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $x>0$ since we're only interested in the  first  quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $x=4,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-12 & =0 \\ 8\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =12 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{12}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the section of the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2}=1$ that lies in the first quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ on the curve at the point where $x=2\sqrt{3},$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ and $x=2\sqrt{3}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot (\frac{2\cdot 2\sqrt{3}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0 \\ 8\sqrt{3}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=2\sqrt{3}$ into the equation of the hyperbola.   

At the point where $x=2\sqrt{3},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(2\sqrt{3})^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2} & =1 \\ 4-{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =3 \\ y & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $y=\sqrt{3},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{3}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2(\sqrt{3}) & =0 \\ 8\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the section of the parabola $3{x}^{2}+4y=1$ that lies in the fourth quadrant.  Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{4}$ on the parabola at the point where $y=-\frac{1}{2},$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+4y & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{x}^{2}+4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (6x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{4}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (6x)+(-\frac{1}{4})\cdot (4) & =0 \\ 6x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into the equation of  the parabola.  

At the point where $y=-\frac{1}{2},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+4y & =1 \\ 3{x}^{2}+4\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) & =1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-2 & =1 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =3 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =3 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $x>0$ since we're only interested in the fourth quadrant.  

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot (1)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-1 & =0 \\ 6\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Related Rate From an Implicitly Defined Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following ellipse: 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1
$$

 

Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=\sqrt{2}$ on the curve at the point $(1,\sqrt2),$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{y}{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=\sqrt{2},$ $x=1,$ and $y=\sqrt2,$ and solve $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$  We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1)+\sqrt{2}\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the curve $x^3-\ln y=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3{x}^{2}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ and $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{1} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the section of the hyperbola 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{3}-\dfrac{y^2}{2}=1
$$

that lies in the first quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=-2$ on the hyperbola at the point where $x=3,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$ at this point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=-2$ and $x=3.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2\cdot 3}{3})-(-2)\cdot y & =0 \\ 2\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-y.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We also want to substitute for $y$, but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=3$ into the equation of the hyperbola.   

At the point where $x=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y > 0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $y= 2,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-y \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$
